Anthropic will soon join them.</li></ul><p><strong>Between the lines: </strong>Anthropic's filing spells out how big the stakes are, devoting more than a quarter of the document to risks.</p><ul><li>The company warns that AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" and that models may try to manipulate the people using them.</li></ul><p><strong>Zoom out:</strong> Each of these three deals is a bet that AI use keeps compounding fast enough to justify the industry's trillions in spending.</p><ul><li>The flip side, however, is that declining use could crack the foundation of America's entire economy.</li></ul><p><strong>The bottom line:</strong> Everyone is on the AI train, whether we want to be or not.</p>Anthropic filed yesterday for what could be the biggest IPO ever, capping a massive day of AI dealmaking that nearly equals 1% of U.S. GDP.

Why it matters: Few industries have ever become so central to the American economy so quickly — and we're watching Wall Street finance the buildout in real time.

Driving the news: Anthropic's long-awaited IPO may seek to raise a record $100 billion.

  • Also yesterday, SpaceX secured $40 billion in debt financing to lease GPUs — the chips that power modern AI — and Meta said it would seek up to $95 billion in financing for its AI buildout.
  • Together, that's roughly $235 billion in a single day — more than the entire U.S. airline industry adds to the economy in a year.

The big picture: AI's appetite for capital has outgrown what any one single part of the financial system can supply.

  • Anthropic alone has committed roughly $750 billion to computing power in the coming years — about seven times what its record-setting IPO may raise.
  • Even private investors are struggling to keep up: OpenAI's record $120 billion funding round took months to close.

Zoom in: Most Americans will be financially exposed to these deals, even if they never buy a share.

  • SpaceX and Meta are already major holdings in the top stock indices that fill pensions, 401(k)s and other retirement plans. Anthropic will soon join them.

Between the lines: Anthropic's filing spells out how big the stakes are, devoting more than a quarter of the document to risks.

  • The company warns that AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" and that models may try to manipulate the people using them.

Zoom out: Each of these three deals is a bet that AI use keeps compounding fast enough to justify the industry's trillions in spending.

  • The flip side, however, is that declining use could crack the foundation of America's entire economy.

The bottom line: Everyone is on the AI train, whether we want to be or not.

The survey had a margin of error for each candidate's result of +/- 3.46 percentage points.</em></p>Republicans fear that Vivek Ramaswamy's explosive attack ad featuring his opponent's estranged mother could cost them the Ohio governor's race, based on new internal polling that shows him falling further behind, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: The poll's findings underscore Republicans' anxiety over Ramaswamy's decision to air the deeply personal attack on Democrat Amy Acton despite warnings from some fellow Republicans that it crossed a line.

Driving the news: The private poll, commissioned by a Republican group and obtained by Axios, found Acton leading Ramaswamy by eight points — up from a two-point lead in the same poll earlier this month, before the ad began circulating on Oct. 19.

  • The ad "is having a significant effect on the gubernatorial race," a memo attached to the poll states.

Catch up quick: The ad at the center of the controversy features Donna Arthur, Acton's estranged mother, who accuses her daughter of lying about her childhood and urges Ohioans not to vote for her.

  • Acton has said she was sexually abused by her stepfather when she was 12 and that her mother sided with her abuser. The stepfather was charged with sexual assault but fled to Pennsylvania, where he died in 2004 as a fugitive.
  • Acton and her brother were removed from their mother's custody. Acton has said she hasn't seen her mother since 1978.

Zoom out: As Axios first reported, Ramaswamy's campaign treated the ad as a game-changer in the campaign for governor, committing $4 million to airing the commercial statewide despite warnings from other Republicans that it could backfire.

  • Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R), who worked closely with Acton when she was the state's health director, said that airing the ad was wrong and urged Ramaswamy to take it down.
  • But President Trump and Vice President Vance backed Ramaswamy. Vance told the bipartisan critics of the ad to "stop whining."

The intrigue: The new poll done for Republicans indicates that the ad was indeed a game-changer — just not the type Ramaswamy's campaign hoped it would be.

  • A memo attached to the poll said that 86% of the survey's 800 respondents said they had seen, read or heard something about the ad.
  • By a 2-to-1 ratio, those who said they were familiar with it said it made them more likely to vote for Acton.

Between the lines: National Republican operatives fear the backlash against Ramaswamy over the ad could also hurt U.S. Sen. Ohio Jon Husted's reelection bid in a state that could be key in determining control of the Senate.

  • Husted has said he wouldn't have run the ad.
  • "Vivek's ad put the whole Republican ticket on defense. He better hope Ohio doesn't decide the Senate majority," said a GOP operative who has been briefed on polling in the race.

The ad was shot months ago, a source familiar with the situation said, but there was internal resistance to running it — with one huge exception.

  • "The candidate is the one pushing for it," a source close to the campaign said.
  • The ad initially was published online because the campaign was testing to see its effectiveness. The ad was sent it to poll respondents to watch on their computers and smartphones to rate, according to the source.
  • "This was not planned. But Vivek got what he wanted," according to the source. "I probably wouldn't have run it."

Yes, but: A separate Suffolk University poll showed a narrower deficit for Ramaswamy — four points, an improvement over Suffolk's previous findings in late September, which found Acton up by nine points.

The other side: Ramaswamy has defended the ad, arguing that Acton has misrepresented her past and avoided addressing substantive issues facing Ohio voters.

What they're saying: A Ramaswamy campaign representative declined to comment.

What's next: Trump is scheduled to campaign in Chillicothe, Ohio, with Ramaswamy and Husted on Wednesday evening.

Axios' Marc Caputo contributed reporting.

The Republican group's internal survey of 800 likely Ohio voters was conducted Oct. 23–26 and found Ramaswamy's support had fallen from 45% earlier this month to 42%, while Acton's climbed from 47% to 50%. The survey had a margin of error for each candidate's result of +/- 3.46 percentage points.

(Photo: Axios)</div><p><strong>Flashback: </strong>Born in the mining town of Dawson, New Mexico, about 140 miles northeast of Santa Fe, Dolores was raised around labor activism, before moving to Stockton, California, as a child. </p><ul><li>She and Chávez founded the National Farm Workers Association in 1962, which later became the United Farm Workers.</li><li>A 2018 PBS documentary <a href="https://www.santafenewmexican.com/news/local_news/film-examines-dolores-huerta-from-jazz-to-s-se-puede/article_2eceeb42-6b38-5371-9c8a-69de237c4d41.html" target="_blank">"Dolores" </a>showed how Huerta moved from a married woman in a middle-class home to a union activist who gave up a comfortable life to join the fight for equality.</li><li>Decades later, she discussed the sexism she faced in the farmworker labor movement despite becoming a Chicana feminist icon on T-shirts, murals and in songs.</li></ul><p><strong>Zoom out:</strong> In her later years, Huerta was sought out by Democrats running for office at all levels, from president to <a href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DRdZGjMgSUJ/" target="_blank">Albuquerque mayor</a>.</p><ul><li>She continued to speak and attend rallies well into her 90s. </li></ul><p><strong>Fun fact: </strong>In 2012, President Obama finally acknowledged Huerta for her role in the creation of his "Yes, we can" slogan during his first presidential campaign.</p><ul><li>"Dolores was very gracious when I told her that I had stolen her slogan," said Obama, who then presented her with the Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor. </li><li>"Knowing her, I'm pleased she left me off easy because Dolores does not play."</li></ul>Dolores Huerta, the pioneering labor organizer who co-founded the United Farm Workers and coined the rallying cry "Sí, se puede," died Wednesday at 96, her family announced on her Instagram account.

Why it matters: The civil rights legend helped lead strikes and boycotts, fought to expand rights for Hispanic Americans and became a powerful kingmaker in politics.

What they're saying: "We are deeply saddened to announce that our beloved mother, Dolores Huerta, has passed away today at the age of 96," her family wrote in a statement posted on Instagram.

  • "As you can imagine, this is an incredibly difficult time for us, and we ask for privacy as we grieve this incredible loss to our family. We know that many of you around the world share in our mourning, and we will be following up on plans to recognize and celebrate her incredible life and legacy."
  • Her cause of death was cancer, per the New York Times.

Zoom in: Huerta worked alongside farmworker leader César Chávez, organizing workers who were routinely subjected to poor labor conditions on farms.

  • The pair founded UFW with fellow activist Gilbert Padilla.
  • Huerta also stood next to Sen. Robert F. Kennedy moments before he was fatally shot after his 1968 California primary win, after having worked to get Mexican American voters to support him.
  • She would befriend the widows of RFK and Martin Luther King Jr., Ethel Kennedy and Coretta Scott King, as they fought together for civil rights.
Dolores Huerta, co-founder of the United Farm Workers group, with a union flag that reads 'Viva La Causa', 1970s. Photo: Cathy Murphy/Getty Images

Catch up quick: Chávez, who died in 1993, allegedly sexually abused multiple women and girls during his time as UFW leader, which only came to light this year following a New York Times investigation.

  • Huerta said that she was raped by Chávez decades ago, becoming the most high-profile figure to accuse him of misconduct.
  • "I carried this secret for as long as I did because building the movement and securing farmworker rights was my life's work," Huerta wrote in a blog post.
  • "I have never identified myself as a victim, but I now understand that I am a survivor — of violence, of sexual abuse, of domineering men who saw me, and other women, as property, or things to control."
  • Huerta said she became pregnant after both encounters with Chávez and arranged for the children to be raised by other families, keeping their births secret.
Huerta speaking to Axios in 2021. (Photo: Axios)

Flashback: Born in the mining town of Dawson, New Mexico, about 140 miles northeast of Santa Fe, Dolores was raised around labor activism, before moving to Stockton, California, as a child.

  • She and Chávez founded the National Farm Workers Association in 1962, which later became the United Farm Workers.
  • A 2018 PBS documentary "Dolores" showed how Huerta moved from a married woman in a middle-class home to a union activist who gave up a comfortable life to join the fight for equality.
  • Decades later, she discussed the sexism she faced in the farmworker labor movement despite becoming a Chicana feminist icon on T-shirts, murals and in songs.

Zoom out: In her later years, Huerta was sought out by Democrats running for office at all levels, from president to Albuquerque mayor.

  • She continued to speak and attend rallies well into her 90s.

Fun fact: In 2012, President Obama finally acknowledged Huerta for her role in the creation of his "Yes, we can" slogan during his first presidential campaign.

  • "Dolores was very gracious when I told her that I had stolen her slogan," said Obama, who then presented her with the Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor.
  • "Knowing her, I'm pleased she left me off easy because Dolores does not play."
